title: A Triumph of Surgery
short: James Herriot and Tricki, the spoiled Pomeranian.
lede: A vet's story about a dog made ill by kindness. The lesson is for the owner, not the animal.
lens: Short answers of 30–40 words and one 50–60 word value-based question.
Know **Tricki** the Pomeranian, **Mrs Pumphrey**, **Hodgkin**, and the vet's decision not to use any medicine.
concepts: **1. Summary.** The narrator, a veterinary surgeon, is asked by **Mrs Pumphrey** to look at her dog **Tricki**, a small Pomeranian. The dog is hugely fat, with bloodshot, rheumy eyes and a lolling tongue, and Mrs Pumphrey worries that he is suffering from **malnutrition**. The vet finds the dog is simply overfed and spoilt: Mrs Pumphrey gives him cream cakes, chocolates, sweets and cod-liver oil, and never lets him exercise. The vet takes Tricki to his surgery and keeps him there for a fortnight. He gives him **no medicine at all** — only water, plenty of exercise and no food for the first two days. Tricki recovers completely, and when Mrs Pumphrey comes to collect him she says it was **a triumph of surgery**. Her friends are so impressed that they begin to bring their own dogs to the vet, and the surgery fills with luxury items sent by the grateful mistress.

**2. Characters.** **Tricki** — a small, spoilt Pomeranian, made ill by overfeeding. **Mrs Pumphrey** — a rich, doting mistress who mistakes overindulgence for love. **The vet (James Herriot)** — practical, kind and shrewd; he understands that the dog's illness is a social problem, not a medical one.
**3. Theme.** Excessive love without discipline harms; and the wisest treatment is sometimes to remove the cause rather than to prescribe medicine.
tricks: - The vet gives **no medicine** — water, fasting and exercise only. That is the point of the story.
- **'A triumph of surgery'** is Mrs Pumphrey's phrase, and it is ironic: no surgery was done.
- Mrs Pumphrey's gifts (eggs, wine, brandy) end up feeding the vet's staff — a comic detail examiners like.
mistakes: - Saying the vet operated on Tricki. There was **no surgery** at all.
- Describing Tricki as a large dog. He is a **small Pomeranian** made fat by overfeeding.
- Missing the irony in the title.

qa.q: Why did Tricki become so ill?
qa.a: Because Mrs Pumphrey overfed him. She gave him cream cakes, chocolates, sweets and cod-liver oil, and never allowed him any exercise. The result was that he became hugely fat, with bloodshot, rheumy eyes and a lolling tongue, and could hardly walk. His illness was caused by indulgence, not by disease.

qa.q: What treatment did the vet give Tricki, and why was it successful?
qa.a: The vet gave no medicine at all. He kept Tricki in his surgery, gave him only water for the first two days, and then plenty of exercise and normal food. The treatment worked because the cause of the illness was overfeeding and lack of exercise, so removing the cause was enough to restore the dog's health.

qa.q: Do you think Mrs Pumphrey was a wise owner? Give reasons.
qa.a: No. She confused love with indulgence. She fed Tricki cream cakes, chocolates and sweets, and never let him exercise, which is why he became dangerously fat and ill. She also ignored the vet's advice about diet and exercise, and continued to send luxury food even after the dog had recovered. A wise owner would have shown affection through discipline and regular activity rather than through food.

qa.q: Mrs Pumphrey calls Tricki's weakness malnutrition and gives him rich food to build him up. As the vet, correct her diagnosis and identify the change needed for recovery.
a: Tricki's illness comes from overfeeding and too little exercise, not a shortage of rich food.
Cakes, sweets and extra supplements have made him overweight and unwell.
The vet removes the cause: a short fast, water, and then simple food and exercise rather than an operation or medicine.

qa.q: A pet owner says that refusing a pet treats is unkind. Use Tricki's recovery to explain why affection also requires limits.
a: Giving Tricki constant treats seemed loving, but it damaged his health.
The vet's restraint and exercise restored him; responsible care means meeting an animal's needs rather than every appetite.

qa.q: What was wrong with Tricki and how had Mrs Pumphrey treated him?
qa.a: Tricki was hugely overfed and listless: Mrs Pumphrey gave him malt, cod-liver oil, Horlicks, cream cakes, chocolates, and even a whole box of eggs with wine and brandy between meals. He had become a bloated, panting little creature with no exercise, so at the surgery James Herriot diagnosed nothing more serious than overeating and lack of discipline.

qa.q: Why did Mrs Pumphrey think Tricki's recovery was ‘a triumph of surgery’? What is ironical about this phrase?
qa.a: Mrs Pumphrey believed the vet had performed some difficult medical feat, so she called the recovery a triumph of surgery. The irony is that there was no surgery and no medicine at all — only water, fasting, exercise and normal food. The real cure was removing the cause (overfeeding), not prescribing anything.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Mrs Pumphrey is alarmed by Tricki's heavy body and dull eyes. The vet realises that she has been giving him cakes, chocolates and supplements, while he gets almost no exercise. At the surgery he first gives the dog water and a period without food.

(a) What is the real cause of Tricki's poor health?
(b) Why does the vet begin with restraint rather than rich food?
(c) What does this treatment suggest about effective care?
a: The dog is overfed and under-exercised; Mrs Pumphrey mistakes the effects of excess for malnutrition.
A short fast removes the immediate cause instead of adding to it, and water keeps the treatment simple.
Care is not always giving more; it may mean removing a harmful habit and allowing gradual, appropriate exercise.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

At the surgery, Tricki spends time with the other dogs and becomes active again. Mrs Pumphrey later sees him running and calls his recovery “a triumph of surgery”, though the vet has not operated on him.

(a) What helps Tricki become active at the surgery?
(b) Why is Mrs Pumphrey's description ironic?
(c) What is the story gently criticising?
a: Simple food, water, exercise and the company of the other dogs help him recover.
She attributes the result to surgery, but there has been no operation; the cure is ordinary care and a change in routine.
The story criticises overindulgence disguised as affection and the assumption that a medical-looking solution is always needed.

qa.q: How does James Herriot cure Tricki, and what does the story say about love and discipline?
a: He takes Tricki away from Mrs Pumphrey, keeps him in the surgery with the other dogs and, for the first two days, gives him no food at all — only water.
On the third day the dog begins to take interest in his bowl, and he is gradually given small amounts of food.
He recovers quickly, learns to play and run with the other dogs, and soon ‘the cure was complete'.
The story shows that love without discipline harms its object: Mrs Pumphrey's affection nearly killed Tricki, while Herriot's firmness restored his health.

qa.q: The vet shares Mrs Pumphrey's food hampers with his partner while Tricki fasts. Does this make him dishonest, or is it part of the humour? Give reasons.
a: It is part of the humour, not real dishonesty — the hampers of eggs, wine and brandy were meant to tempt Tricki, and giving them to a fasting dog would have undone the cure.
The vet and his partner enjoying the food while Tricki slimmed down on water is the story's running joke: the rich food fattens everyone except the patient.
What matters is that Tricki recovered fully; the vet's method, if not his manners, was exactly right.

qa.q: Why is the title “A Triumph of Surgery” ironic, and what does Tricki's treatment reveal about the difference between indulgence and care?
a: Mrs Pumphrey uses the title to celebrate Tricki's recovery, but James Herriot performs no surgery and gives him no medicine.
Tricki's illness was caused by excess food and lack of exercise, so the vet's first step is to stop the treats and let the dog rest and drink water.
As Tricki gains strength, simple food, movement and the company of other dogs restore his health.
The humour exposes Mrs Pumphrey's mistake: affection without judgement can harm. Good care sometimes means setting limits instead of giving more.

mcq.q: Tricki was a: (a) small Pomeranian (b) large Alsatian (c) greyhound (d) spaniel
mcq.a: **(a) a small Pomeranian**, spoilt and overfed by Mrs Pumphrey.

mcq.q: The vet treated Tricki with: (a) an operation (b) antibiotics (c) cod-liver oil (d) no medicine, only water and exercise
mcq.a: **(d) no medicine at all** — water, fasting at first, then exercise and a normal diet.

mcq.q: The phrase 'a triumph of surgery' is spoken by: (a) Mrs Pumphrey (b) the vet (c) Mrs Pumphrey's friends (d) Tricki
mcq.a: **(a) Mrs Pumphrey**, when she came to collect the recovered dog.

mcq.q: What is the main cause of Tricki's illness? (a) A broken leg (b) A shortage of toys (c) Overfeeding and too little exercise (d) An attack by another dog
mcq.a: **(c) Overfeeding and too little exercise.** Mrs Pumphrey's constant treats and lack of exercise have made him unwell.

mcq.q: Who narrates “A Triumph of Surgery”? (a) Mrs Pumphrey's neighbour (b) The veterinary surgeon (c) Tricki (d) The kennel attendant
mcq.a: **(b) The veterinary surgeon.** James Herriot narrates the story of treating Tricki.

mcq.q: Tricki was: (a) a bulldog  (b) a cat  (c) a poodle  (d) a Pomeranian
mcq.a: **(d) a Pomeranian.** A small dog pampered into illness by his wealthy owner.

mcq.q: Mrs Pumphrey sent Tricki to the surgery with: (a) only water  (b) eggs, wine and brandy  (c) medicines  (d) toys
mcq.a: **(b) eggs, wine and brandy.** She sent two dozen eggs, two bottles of wine and a bottle of brandy.

mcq.q: Tricki recovered fully in: (a) two days (b) a month (c) a fortnight (d) six months
mcq.a: **(c) a fortnight.** Two weeks of water, exercise and plain food cured what rich food had caused.

trend: The cause of Tricki's illness and the vet's treatment are asked almost every year; the value-based question on Mrs Pumphrey's wisdom recurs.
onepager: - James Herriot; Tricki the Pomeranian; Mrs Pumphrey overfeeds him.
- The vet gives no medicine — water, fasting, then exercise and normal food.
- Tricki recovers in a fortnight; Mrs Pumphrey calls it a triumph of surgery.
- Theme: love without discipline harms; remove the cause rather than prescribe.
task: Write the story in six sentences, then add one sentence on the lesson for pet owners. Seven sentences is exactly the length of a 50–60 word answer.
steps: 1. Begin with the **problem**: Mrs Pumphrey'sTricki, overfed and listless, 'like a bloated sausage'.
2. Give **Dr Herriot's diagnosis and plan** — no medicine, only discipline, company and a strict diet at the surgery.
3. Show the **change in order**: two days nothing, then Tricki joins the other dogs, then he is racing about with them.
4. Close with Mrs Pumphrey's tearful reunion and her mistaken **'triumph of surgery'** — the surgery was diet and exercise, not an operation.

title: The Thief's Story
short: Ruskin Bond: a small thief, a kind writer, and a changed mind.
lede: A story about a conscience waking up. The moment on the platform is the heart of the answer.
lens: Short answers and a value-based question on why the thief came back.
**Anil** the struggling writer; the thief is **fifteen** and takes the name **Hari Singh**.
concepts: **1. Summary.** The narrator is a fairly successful thief, still only fifteen but already experienced. He meets **Anil**, a tall, lean, easy-going young writer at a wrestling match, and decides to rob him. He gives his name as **Hari Singh** and changes it every month to escape the police. Anil takes him in as a servant, but he pays him irregularly and mostly in food, so there is little to steal. The narrator learns to write his name and to write whole sentences from Anil, and realises that once he can write like an educated man there will be no limit to what he can achieve. One night the thief steals **six hundred rupees** from under Anil's mattress and runs to the station to catch the Lucknow Express. As the train moves out, he finds he cannot board it — he has no ticket and no one to help him. He walks aimlessly in the rain, finds the stolen notes are **wet and ruined**, and realises that Anil will not be angry for the loss of money but for the loss of trust. He goes back, puts the damp notes under the mattress, and lies down. In the morning Anil gives him a **fifty-rupee note** and says he will pay him regularly; the note is still damp, but Anil says nothing. The narrator knows that Anil knew everything, and that he has been given a second chance.

**2. Characters.** **The thief (Hari Singh)** — young, experienced in petty theft, but still capable of shame; he is the narrator. **Anil** — a kind, careless, easy-going writer who trusts people, and whose trust is what reforms the boy.
**3. Theme.** Trust and kindness can reform a person where punishment cannot; and education opens a better path than crime.
tricks: - **The thief returns because of loss of trust, not loss of money.** That sentence is the standard 3-mark answer.
- Anil **knows** the notes were stolen — he says nothing, which is the act of kindness.
- The name **Hari Singh** changes every month to dodge the police.
mistakes: - Saying Anil punished him. He **says nothing** and pays him regularly instead.
- Saying the notes were safe. They were **wet and ruined** by the rain.
- Describing Anil as rich. He is a **struggling writer** who paid irregularly.

qa.q: Why did the thief return to Anil?
qa.a: Because while walking in the rain he realised that Anil would not be grieved by the loss of money — Anil was careless about money — but he would be grieved by the loss of trust. The thief understood that he had destroyed something more valuable than the six hundred rupees, and that realisation, along with the thought of what he was learning from Anil, brought him back.

qa.q: What did the thief learn from Anil, and why was it important to him?
qa.a: Anil taught him to write his name, and then to write whole sentences. The thief realised that once he could write like an educated man there would be no limit to what he could achieve — he could earn respectably instead of stealing small amounts. Education offered him a future that crime could not.

qa.q: Did Anil know that the money had been stolen? How can you tell?
qa.a: Yes, he knew. The fifty-rupee note he gave the thief in the morning was still damp from the rain, and Anil said nothing about it. His silence, and his decision to pay the boy regularly from that day, show that he understood what had happened and chose to give the boy a second chance rather than to accuse him.

qa.q: Hari can keep the stolen money and disappear, yet he returns to Anil before morning. Explain how the prospect of education influences that decision.
a: Hari has begun to see writing as a route to a different life, beyond the quick money available through theft.
Returning risks losing the notes, but stealing from Anil would also betray the trust that made learning possible.
He chooses the chance of education and a new start over the immediate gain; the decision shows his conscience beginning to change.

qa.q: Anil gives Hari food, shelter and lessons rather than treating him as a criminal. What does Hari's response show about the effect of trust?
a: Anil's trust gives Hari a reason to imagine a future that does not depend on stealing.
Hari still gives in to temptation, but the kindness makes him feel shame and return the money; trust helps awaken his conscience.

qa.q: Why does Hari Singh come back to Anil after stealing the money?
a: He gets on the train at Lucknow but does not board it; he cannot bring himself to break away from Anil.
He knows that stealing is easy but education would change his life, and Anil was the only person teaching him to read and write.
He also fears that if he leaves, the wet notes will be all he has, and the chance to become ‘a big man' will be gone.
So he returns, puts the notes back under the mattress, and accepts Anil's quiet forgiveness, which we never see refused.

qa.q: Why could the thief not board the train to Lucknow after stealing the money?
qa.a: He reached the station just as the Lucknow Express was moving out and could not board it — he had no ticket and no idea where to spend the night. Left alone on the platform in the rain, with the notes getting damp, he began to think about Anil's trust instead of the money. The missed train gave his conscience the time it needed.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Hari takes Anil's money and reaches the railway station, intending to leave for Lucknow. In the rain he does not board the train. Before morning he returns, puts the damp notes back, and waits for Anil to wake.

(a) What opportunity does Hari abandon at the station?
(b) What do his actions after returning show?
(c) Why is Anil's trust important to this change?
a: He gives up the immediate escape to Lucknow with the stolen money.
Returning the damp notes shows remorse and a choice to repair the betrayal rather than run away.
Anil's earlier kindness and offer to teach him have made the relationship worth preserving; Hari now values that trust and the education it brings.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Anil does not confront Hari about the missing money. The next morning he gives him a note and says they will begin writing sentences. Hari notices that the note is still damp from the rain.

(a) What does the damp note allow Hari to realise?
(b) How does Anil respond to the theft?
(c) What does the offer of writing lessons suggest about Anil's purpose?
a: Hari understands that Anil has likely noticed the theft and knows the money has been returned wet.
Anil does not shame or punish him; he quietly restores the money and continues to treat Hari with trust.
He is offering Hari a constructive future through education, not merely a job as a servant.

qa.q: Describe Anil's character and how he changes Hari Singh.
a: Anil is a young, easy-going writer who earns irregularly, lives simply and is generous, patient and trusting without being foolish.
He feeds Hari Singh and teaches him to cook, to write his name and to add numbers, never asking where the boy came from.
He knows the money was stolen but says nothing about it; instead he gives the boy a fifty-rupee note and says he will pay him regularly.
That trust shames Hari Singh into honesty: for the first time someone believes in him, and he chooses education and work over theft.

qa.q: Anil's ‘easy’ attitude to money is called his most appealing quality. How does this quality both invite the theft and reform the thief?
a: It invites the theft because Anil leaves money carelessly — under the mattress, in plain sight — making stealing easy for a boy who lives by it.
It reforms the thief because this same carelessness shows complete trust: Anil would grieve the loss of trust, not of money.
The thief realises that stealing from a man who trusts him costs more than it gains — Anil's ease with money teaches him that some things matter more than money.

qa.q: How does Anil's trust change Hari Singh, and why is the decision to return more important than the money itself?
a: Hari begins as an experienced young thief who changes his name regularly and intends to rob Anil.
Anil offers him food and shelter, pays him, and begins teaching him to read and write; the lessons reveal a lawful path beyond petty theft.
Hari steals the notes, but cannot bring himself to board the train. He returns them even though he could have escaped with the money.
The return marks a moral choice: he values Anil's trust and his chance to learn more than a short-lived gain. Anil's silence gives that change room to grow.

mcq.q: The thief gave his name as: (a) Anil (b) Ruskin (c) Arun (d) Hari Singh
mcq.a: **(d) Hari Singh**, and he changed his name every month to escape the police.

mcq.q: Anil was a: (a) wrestler (b) struggling writer (c) moneylender (d) shopkeeper
mcq.a: **(b) a struggling writer** — tall, lean and easy-going.

mcq.q: The thief returned the money because: (a) he realised he had lost Anil's trust (b) he was caught (c) he feared the police (d) the notes were ruined
mcq.a: **(a) he realised he had lost Anil's trust**, which mattered more than the money.

mcq.q: What new skill does Anil begin teaching Hari? (a) Repairing locks (b) Driving a train (c) Writing sentences (d) Keeping accounts for a shop
mcq.a: **(c) Writing sentences.** Anil's lessons offer Hari a path toward education and a different future.

mcq.q: What does Hari do with the stolen money before Anil wakes? (a) He returns it to its place (b) He gives it to the police (c) He hides it at the station (d) He spends it on food
mcq.a: **(a) He returns it to its place.** He puts the damp notes back after deciding not to leave.

mcq.q: Hari Singh says that he changes his name: (a) every year  (b) never  (c) every month to hide from the police and old employers  (d) every week
mcq.a: **(c) every month.** It is the habit of a thief who never stays long in one place or with one name.

mcq.q: Anil earned his living by: (a) working in a shop  (b) writing  (c) teaching  (d) wrestling
mcq.a: **(b) writing.** He wrote for magazines, which is why his income was irregular.

mcq.q: The amount the thief stole from Anil was: (a) 60 rupees (b) 6,000 rupees (c) 100 rupees (d) 600 rupees
mcq.a: **(d) 600 rupees.** Anil had earned it by selling a book to a publisher the previous day.

trend: Why the thief came back, and whether Anil knew, alternate as the set questions; the value of education to the thief recurs.
onepager: - Ruskin Bond; the thief is 15 and calls himself Hari Singh, changing the name monthly.
- Anil, a kind struggling writer, teaches him to write his name and sentences.
- He steals ₹600, cannot board the train, and the notes get ruined in the rain.
- He returns because Anil would grieve the loss of trust, not of money.
- Anil knows, says nothing, and pays him regularly — a second chance.
task: Write the moment on the platform in four sentences, then two sentences on why he turned back. Six sentences is a complete value-based answer.
steps: 1. Name the **narrator and his situation** — Hari Singh, a fifteen-year-old thief, and Anil, the wrestler-writer he plans to rob.
2. Describe the **robbery**: six hundred rupees taken while Anil sleeps, and the train Hari Singh fails to board.
3. Explain the **change of heart** — Anil's trust, the promise to teach him to read and write, and the fear of losing the chance to become 'a respected man'.
4. Close with the **note he leaves**, the jalebis, and the fact that Anil already knew: 'I knew he'd give the money back… he did look honest.'

title: The Midnight Visitor
short: Robert Arthur: Ausable the unlikely secret agent and a invented balcony.
lede: A spy story with no guns — the hero wins with words and quick thinking.
lens: Short answers and a character question on Ausable.
**Ausable**, **Max**, and the invented **balcony** are the three names to know.
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Ausable** is a secret agent, but he is nothing like the popular image of one: he is very fat, lives in a small, musty room on the top floor of a gloomy French hotel, and speaks French and German only passably. He has just been given an important report about some missiles. **Max**, a rival agent, is waiting in his room with a pistol, having entered by a passkey, and demands the report. At that moment there is a knock at the door. Ausable says it is the police, whom he has called because someone has been trying to enter his room through the **balcony** — a balcony that Max believes exists because Ausable describes it in such detail, and because Max himself has climbed in through a window that he thought led to a balcony. Panicking, Max steps backwards through the window onto a balcony that is not there, and falls six storeys to his death. The knock turns out to be a waiter bringing a drink that Ausable had ordered.

**2. Characters.** **Ausable** — fat, unglamorous, quick-witted; he invents a balcony and a police call in seconds and saves himself without firing a shot. **Max** — a slender, sinister rival agent, confident and armed, but out-thought.
**3. Theme.** Intelligence and presence of mind are more valuable than weapons; and appearances are misleading.
tricks: - Ausable never had a balcony and never called the police — **both are inventions**. Say so explicitly.
- The waiter with the drink is the comic reveal; do not forget it.
- Max dies because he **believes** the story, not because Ausable attacks him.
mistakes: - Saying Ausable called the police. The knock was **a waiter** with the drink he had ordered.
- Saying there was a real balcony. There was **none** — Ausable invented it.
- Describing Ausable as a typical dashing spy. He is **fat and unglamorous** — that is the point.

qa.q: How did Ausable get rid of Max?
qa.a: Ausable invented a balcony outside his window and told Max that he had complained twice to the hotel management about people entering his room through it. When the knock came at the door, he said it was the police, whom he had called. Max, panicking, said he would wait on the balcony and jumped backwards through the window — onto a balcony that did not exist — and fell six storeys to his death.

qa.q: How is Ausable different from the usual picture of a secret agent?
qa.a: He is very fat and sloppy, and lives in a small, musty room on the top floor of a gloomy French hotel, which does not fit the image of a dashing spy. He speaks French and German only passably, and has never fired a shot or been involved in dramatic action. Yet he is a highly effective agent, because he uses his wits rather than weapons.

qa.q: What was the knock at the door?
qa.a: It was a waiter bringing the drink that Ausable had ordered before Max arrived. Ausable had already mentioned expecting a drink, so when the knock came he was able to pretend it was the police he had called. The reveal that it was only a waiter is the story's comic ending.

qa.q: Fowler expects a secret agent to be dramatic, but Ausable looks ordinary. Explain how the story uses this mismatch to change Fowler's idea of a spy.
a: Ausable is fat and unglamorous, unlike the romantic spy Fowler had imagined.
His quick thinking under pressure proves more useful than a dramatic appearance or weapon.
Fowler sees that intelligence and control of a situation, not looks, make Ausable an effective agent.

qa.q: Max has a pistol, while Ausable has no weapon ready. Name the two invented details Ausable uses to make Max act against his own interests.
a: Ausable invents a balcony outside the window and says that the knock at the door is the police.
Max believes both claims, tries to escape by the nonexistent balcony, and falls when he jumps out of the window.

qa.q: How does Ausable outwit Max?
a: Ausable tells Max and Fowler that his room has a balcony, and that someone has already got into it; this makes Max anxious.
When the waiter knocks, Ausable says it must be the police, whom he has asked to check on him.
Max backs towards the window, steps out onto what he believes is the balcony, and falls to his death — there is no balcony at all.
Ausable had invented the whole story, and his quick thinking removes a dangerous rival without a shot being fired.

qa.q: Why did Fowler feel disappointed when he first met Ausable? How had his opinion changed by the end?
qa.a: Fowler, a young writer, expected a romantic, mysterious secret agent and found instead a very fat, sloppy man in a cheap French hotel — nothing like the films. By the end his disappointment turns to admiration: Ausable defeats an armed rival with nothing but two invented stories, proving that real spycraft is presence of mind, not glamour.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Max waits in Ausable's room and demands the secret report. Ausable calmly claims that there is a balcony outside the window and that the police have come. The knock is actually made by a waiter carrying a drink.

(a) What is Max trying to obtain?
(b) Which part of Ausable's story about the room is invented?
(c) Why does the waiter’s knock help Ausable?
a: Max wants the important report about the missiles.
There is no balcony outside the window; Ausable invents it to make Max think he has an escape route.
Max believes Ausable's claim that the police are at the door and panics, so the ordinary knock gives the bluff urgency.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Fowler comes to meet an agent but finds a quiet hotel room and an armed rival. Ausable remains calm, invents a detail about the building, and gives Max a reason to hurry toward the window.

(a) What quality does Ausable show?
(b) Why is Max's weapon not enough to give him control?
(c) What does the scene suggest about presence of mind?
a: Ausable shows composure and quick improvisation under threat.
Max has a pistol, but he accepts Ausable's false story and lets fear dictate his next move.
A clear mind can turn an opponent's assumptions against him; a weapon alone does not guarantee control.

qa.q: What is ironic about Ausable as a secret agent?
a: Fowler, a writer, expects a secret agent to be slim, romantic and mysterious — a figure out of a thriller.
Instead he meets a fat, sloppy man with a thick accent, in a shabby room on the sixth floor of a French hotel.
This plain, unimpressive man is the one who outwits an armed spy by using only his wits and a fabricated story.
The irony is that the real professional is dull and clever, while the romantic picture exists only in books — which is the point of the story.

qa.q: Ausable invents the balcony and the police visit within seconds. What does this presence of mind tell us about real spycraft versus film spycraft?
a: Film spycraft is weapons, chases and gadgets; Ausable has none of these — only his wits.
In seconds he reads Max's fear (exposure) and builds a trap from it: a balcony that does not exist and policemen who are really a waiter.
The story's point is that intelligence beats intimidation — Max holds the gun, but Ausable holds the situation. That is why appearances mislead.

qa.q: How does Ausable defeat Max without using a weapon, and what does Fowler learn from the encounter?
a: Max enters with a pistol and expects Ausable to hand over the missile report, putting the agent in immediate danger.
Ausable stays calm and invents a balcony outside the window, then claims the police are at the door. The actual visitor is a waiter with a drink.
Max believes the fabricated escape route and jumps out of the window when he hears the knock; Ausable has outwitted him with words rather than force.

Fowler's romantic expectations give way to respect for Ausable's intelligence. The story shows that presence of mind and knowledge of an opponent's assumptions can matter more than appearance or weapons.

mcq.q: Ausable is described as: (a) very fat and sloppy (b) tall and handsome (c) thin and sinister (d) old and blind
mcq.a: **(a) very fat and sloppy** — deliberately unlike the usual picture of a secret agent.

mcq.a: **(b) a waiter with a drink** that Ausable had ordered.

mcq.a: **(c) he jumped backwards through the window onto a balcony that did not exist**, and fell six storeys.

mcq.a: **(d) A pistol.** Max uses it to threaten Ausable and demand the report.

mcq.a: **(a) A balcony beyond the window.** There is no balcony; the false detail is part of Ausable's bluff.

mcq.q: Ausable told Max that the balcony he saw belonged to: (a) Ausable's own room  (b) the next apartment  (c) the hotel manager  (d) nobody
mcq.a: **(b) the next apartment.** The lie made Max step out of the window and fall.

mcq.q: Fowler, the writer, expected a secret agent to be: (a) fat and foolish  (b) elderly and rich  (c) romantic and mysterious  (d) an Indian
mcq.a: **(c) romantic and mysterious.** Ausable, fat and unglamorous, is a deliberate contrast.

mcq.q: Max entered Ausable's room to steal: (a) money (b) a passport (c) a gun (d) a report about new missiles
mcq.a: **(d) a report about new missiles.** The secret papers were the reason for the midnight visit.

title: A Question of Trust
short: Victor Canning: Horace Danby robbed by a thief posing as the lady of the house.
lede: A burglar out-burgled. The woman in red is one of the great reveals in the supplementary reader.
lens: Short answers and a value-based question on whether the lady was right to trick Horace.
**Horace Danby**, **Shotover Grange**, and the **woman in red** are the key names.
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Horace Danby** was a good and respectable man, about fifty and unmarried, who made locks and was successful enough to have two people help him. But he was not completely honest: he robbed a safe every year, planning each robbery carefully, so that the money lasted twelve months. He robbed only rich people, and never robbed anyone poor. This year he had planned to rob the safe at **Shotover Grange**, which contained about fifteen thousand pounds' worth of jewels. He had studied the house for two weeks and knew that the family was in London. He entered, cut the wires of the burglar alarm, and found the safe — but it had a lock he had not seen before. As he worked, a **young woman dressed in red** appeared, saying she had come home just in time. She spoke as the lady of the house, said her husband was away and that the jewels were needed for a party that night, and asked Horace to open the safe for her, saying she had forgotten the number. She also threatened to call the police. Horace, afraid of prison, opened the safe and gave her the jewels, and left without his gloves. Two days later he was arrested, because he had left his **fingerprints** all over the room. In prison he is the assistant librarian, and he is angry when anyone mentions honour among thieves.

**2. Characters.** **Horace Danby** — respectable, careful, a lover of rare and expensive books, and a thief only once a year. **The young woman in red** — calm, confident, quick-thinking, and herself a burglar who had been waiting for exactly this opportunity.
**3. Theme.** Honour among thieves does not exist; and overconfidence makes even a careful man careless.
tricks: - **He forgot his gloves** because he believed her story — that detail explains the arrest.
- The woman's trick worked because she **pretended to be in trouble herself** and asked for help.
- The last line — 'honour among thieves' — is the standard closing point of any long answer.
mistakes: - Saying the woman was the owner's wife. She was **another thief**, who had planned to rob the same house.
- Saying Horace was arrested at the house. He was arrested **two days later**, because of the fingerprints.
- Describing Horace as a habitual criminal. He robbed **once a year** and was otherwise respectable.

qa.q: How did the young woman manage to get the jewels from Horace?
qa.a: She appeared while he was working on the safe and spoke to him as if she were the lady of the house, saying she had arrived home just in time. She told him that the jewels were needed that evening for a party, that she had forgotten the number of the safe, and that if he did not open it for her she would have to call the police. Afraid of being sent to prison, Horace opened the safe and handed her the jewels, and she let him go. She was herself a burglar, who had been waiting for her chance.

qa.q: Why was Horace arrested?
qa.a: Because he had left his fingerprints all over the room. When the young woman told him her story and asked him to open the safe, he was so relieved and so eager to escape that he forgot to put on his gloves. Two days later the police arrested him, using the fingerprints as evidence.

qa.q: Do you think the young lady was right in tricking Horace? Give reasons.
qa.a: No. She used another person's crime to cover her own, and she let an innocent-seeming man take the blame. Although Horace was himself a thief, she could have simply left the house instead of framing him. Her action shows that 'honour among thieves' does not exist — she was willing to send him to prison to protect herself and keep the jewels.

qa.q: Horace Danby is usually careful and wears gloves, but he is arrested after the robbery at Shotover Grange. Explain how trusting the woman changes his precautions.
a: Horace believes the woman is the house's owner and accepts her claim that she has forgotten the safe combination.
He follows her request to open the safe and removes his gloves, leaving fingerprints behind.
His usual care fails because he trusts a stranger and lets the apparent emergency override his plan.

qa.q: The woman in red seems confident and familiar with the house. What clues should have made Horace question her story, and what does he do instead?
a: Horace has no independent proof that she owns Shotover Grange; her calm manner and claim of authority are not evidence.
He accepts her story and opens the safe for her, allowing another thief to use his skills.

qa.q: How is Horace Danby trapped by the young woman at Shotover Grange?
a: She finds him unlocking the door, and calmly claims to be the lady of the house who has forgotten her jewels upstairs.
Horace helps her open the door, and she watches him take the jewels from the safe and lets him go with them.
Because she saw him handle the safe, her fingerprints are not needed: he has left a clean set of prints all over the house.
The police find his fingerprints and arrest him, while the real thief, who had read the family's letters in the hall, escapes.

qa.q: Why did Horace Danby rob only once a year, and what did he do with the money?
qa.a: Horace was otherwise a good, respectable locksmith who loved rare and expensive books but could not afford them honestly. So he robbed one safe a year — carefully planned, always enough to last twelve months — and spent the money secretly through an agent on first editions for his library. Crime, for him, was a yearly subscription to his hobby.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Horace has studied the house and taken precautions for his annual robbery. A woman appears, says she is the lady of the house, and asks him to open the safe because she has forgotten the combination. Horace removes his gloves while helping her.

(a) Why does Horace agree to open the safe?
(b) What practical mistake does he make?
(c) How does the encounter lead to his arrest?
a: He believes the woman is the owner and accepts her request as genuine.
He removes his gloves, abandoning a precaution that would have protected him from leaving fingerprints.
The police later identify his fingerprints at the safe; the woman has taken the jewels and left Horace to answer for the robbery.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Horace regards himself as respectable and robs only rich households once a year. At Shotover Grange, a woman takes the jewels and leaves him behind. He is arrested, while the woman is not found.

(a) Why does Horace think of himself as respectable?
(b) What irony lies in the outcome?
(c) What warning does the episode give about trust?
a: He maintains an ordinary life as a successful locksmith and limits his thefts to one planned robbery each year, though he is still a criminal.
He considers himself a careful thief but is deceived by another thief and becomes the only person arrested.
A confident appearance is not proof of honesty; Horace should have questioned the stranger's story rather than trusting it.

qa.q: What is the irony in ‘A Question of Trust'?
a: Horace Danby is a respectable locksmith and a successful crook who plans his robberies carefully for a year.
The young woman who tricks him is not a lady but a thief who does no planning at all: she simply reads the letters in the hall, walks in and walks out with the jewels.
Horace is caught by his own fingerprints while she leaves none, because she wore gloves and was never seen as a thief.
The title's irony is double: Horace trusted the wrong person, and the police trust only the evidence, so the guiltiest person goes free.

qa.q: ‘Honour among thieves does not exist.’ How does the ending prove this? Do you feel any sympathy for Horace?
a: The young woman in red is herself a thief; she uses Horace to open the safe, takes the jewels, and leaves him to be caught by his own fingerprints. One thief betrays another without a second thought.

Some sympathy is natural — Horace is polite, careful and robbed by a cleverer criminal — but the story withholds full pity: he chose crime freely, and a thief complaining of being robbed is the joke the title promises.

qa.q: How does the woman in red turn Horace Danby's careful plan against him, and what does the ending say about his idea of honour?
a: Horace plans the Shotover Grange robbery carefully, believing his experience as a locksmith and his precautions will keep him safe.
The woman calmly presents herself as the owner and claims she needs the safe opened. Horace trusts her and removes his gloves while helping.
She takes the jewels, while his fingerprints connect him to the safe and lead to his arrest. His care is defeated by misplaced trust.
Horace's belief that he is an honourable thief does not protect him; the other criminal has no loyalty to him. The ending makes his moral code look self-serving and naïve.

mcq.q: Horace Danby robbed a safe: (a) every month (b) once a year (c) whenever he needed money (d) only from the rich and the poor alike
mcq.a: **(b) once a year**, planning each robbery carefully so that the money lasted twelve months.

mcq.q: The safe that Horace planned to rob was at: (a) Shotover Grange (b) Shotover House (c) a London bank (d) a jeweller's shop
mcq.a: **(a) Shotover Grange**, which contained about fifteen thousand pounds' worth of jewels.

mcq.q: Horace was arrested because: (a) the woman informed the police (b) he dropped his tools (c) he was seen by a servant (d) he left his fingerprints
mcq.a: **(d) he left his fingerprints** all over the room — he had forgotten to wear gloves.

mcq.q: What precaution does Horace abandon when he opens the safe for the woman? (a) He switches off the lights (b) He leaves his tools outside (c) He removes his gloves (d) He locks the front door
mcq.a: **(c) He removes his gloves.** His fingerprints are left at the safe and help lead to his arrest.

mcq.q: What is Horace Danby's trade? (a) He sells flowers (b) He trains horses (c) He makes locks (d) He repairs watches
mcq.a: **(c) He makes locks.** His work makes him knowledgeable about safes and security.

mcq.q: Horace Danby's hobby was: (a) painting  (b) collecting rare and expensive books  (c) gardening  (d) singing
mcq.a: **(b) collecting rare and expensive books.** It was the motive for his yearly robbery.

mcq.q: Horace was arrested for robbing: (a) Shotover Grange  (b) a bank  (c) a bookshop  (d) a museum
mcq.a: **(a) Shotover Grange.** His fingerprints all over the house were the evidence.

mcq.q: The jewels at Shotover Grange were said to be worth about: (a) fifteen hundred pounds (b) one hundred and fifty thousand pounds (c) five hundred pounds (d) fifteen thousand pounds
mcq.a: **(d) fifteen thousand pounds.** A year's worth of rare books for Horace — and for the lady in red.

2. Give the **plan and the execution**: the dogs shut away, the safe in the drawing room, the very good lock that takes him too long.

title: Footprints without Feet
short: H. G. Wells: Griffin the invisible scientist becomes a hunted lawless man.
lede: A science-fiction story with a moral: brilliant science without conscience makes a criminal.
lens: Short answers and a long answer on whether Griffin was a brilliant scientist or a lawless person.
**Griffin**, and the three places he goes: **London, Iping, and back to London**.
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Griffin** was a brilliant scientist who had carried out experiment after experiment to prove that the human body could become invisible, and finally swallowed certain rare drugs, so that his body became as transparent as a sheet of glass, though as hard to see. His landlord disliked him and was trying to eject him, so in revenge Griffin set fire to the house and, to escape without being seen, removed his clothes. He became a homeless wanderer without clothes, without money and quite invisible. He went to a big London store, where he put on clothes, ate and slept, and then had to strip again before the store opened. He went to a theatrical company in Drury Lane, bandaged his face to hide his invisibility, robbed the shopkeeper there, and escaped to **Iping** village by train. He booked two rooms at the inn and paid the landlord, **Mr Hall**, in advance. There he experimented further, and strange things began to happen: the landlady **Mrs Hall** found the scientist's door open and his room empty, then a chair became alive and pushed her and her husband out of the room and slammed the door. When the landlord asked for rent, Griffin threw off his bandages and whiskers, and became a headless man. The village constable, **Mr Jaffers**, came to arrest him; Griffin removed his clothes one by one, and Jaffers found himself hitting a man he could not see, and was knocked unconscious. Griffin escaped again, a lawless man wandering without clothes, money, home or friends.

**2. Characters.** **Griffin** — a brilliant but lawless scientist; his discovery is remarkable, but he uses it for revenge and theft. **Mr and Mrs Hall** — the innkeepers at Iping. **Mr Jaffers** — the village constable.
**3. Theme.** Scientific brilliance without moral responsibility produces a danger to society; and a person who lives outside the law ends up entirely alone.
tricks: - **Two words describe him: brilliant and lawless.** Every long answer on Griffin needs both.
- He became invisible by **swallowing rare drugs**, then had to remove his clothes to stay unseen.
- The chair scene in Mrs Hall's room is the most frequently extracted passage.
mistakes: - Saying Griffin was invisible by birth. He made himself invisible by **swallowing rare drugs**.
- Placing the inn in London. It is in **Iping**, a village.
- Forgetting that he set fire to the landlord's house — the first evidence of his lawlessness.

qa.q: How did Griffin become invisible?
qa.a: He was a brilliant scientist who carried out experiment after experiment to prove that the human body could be made invisible, and at last he swallowed certain rare drugs. His body became as transparent as a sheet of glass, though still as hard to see. To avoid being seen he also had to remove his clothes, which left him naked, homeless and penniless in the middle of winter.

qa.q: Describe what happened at the inn in Iping.
qa.a: Griffin booked two rooms and paid Mr Hall in advance, but behaved strangely, refusing company and shutting himself in. When Mrs Hall went to his room she found the door open and the room empty, with the clothes he had been wearing scattered about. Suddenly a hat hopped off the bedpost and struck her face, and then a chair became alive, pushed both her and her husband out of the room and slammed and locked the door behind them. Mrs Hall was convinced the room was haunted by spirits.

qa.q: Griffin is a brilliant scientist, but the story presents him as a threat to the people around him. Explain why invisibility does not make him admirable.
a: Griffin's discovery of invisibility is scientifically remarkable, but he uses it for selfish and unlawful acts.
He sets fire to his landlord's house, steals clothes and money, and harms people who try to stop him.
The story separates scientific ability from character: knowledge without responsibility can make someone dangerous.

qa.q: A student claims that an invisible person could move through a town without leaving evidence. Use Griffin's footprints at Iping to correct this claim.
a: Invisibility hides Griffin's body, but it does not remove the physical marks his feet make in wet mud.
The moving footprints alert the villagers that someone is there, showing that an invisible person can still leave evidence.

qa.q: Why does Griffin fail as an invisible man?
a: He discovers how to make the human body transparent, but he does not discover how to make it visible again, and he cannot reverse his experiment.
Invisibility leaves him without clothes, food and shelter; he is hungry, cold and hunted everywhere.
His behavior turns violent: he sets fire to his landlord's house, assaults people who get in his way and steals to survive.
Finally he is attacked by the crowd in the inn, and his cloak is torn off, revealing an empty space where a man should be.

qa.q: Why did Griffin burn his landlord's house? What does this first crime tell us about him?
qa.a: Griffin burnt the house in revenge because his landlord tried to eject him. This first crime tells us that Griffin answers every obstacle with destruction — he has brilliance without conscience. The pattern never changes: robbery, assault and finally beating Constable Jaffers follow from the same lawless temper.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Griffin's body cannot be seen, yet in muddy streets at Iping a line of footprints appears to move without a visible person. The villagers follow the marks and become alarmed.

(a) What do the footprints reveal?
(b) Why do the people find them frightening?
(c) What limit of Griffin's experiment do they expose?
a: They reveal Griffin's passage even though the rest of him is invisible.
The marks seem to move on their own because no body can be seen making them.
Invisibility does not erase every physical trace: his feet still press into wet ground and leave tracks.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Griffin removes his clothes to become invisible, but he still needs food, shelter and warmth. In Iping he takes clothes and money and frightens the people who try to question him.

(a) Why must Griffin obtain clothes after becoming invisible?
(b) What does his conduct at Iping show about him?
(c) What central conflict does the story raise?
a: Without clothes, an invisible person is exposed to cold and cannot pass unnoticed in ordinary weather or surroundings.
Griffin acts selfishly and violently, using his discovery to intimidate people instead of helping them.
The story asks what happens when scientific power is separated from ethical responsibility and regard for others.

qa.q: Describe Griffin's character and what the story says about the misuse of science.
a: Griffin is a brilliant scientist, but he is selfish, violent and dishonest: he uses his discovery to rob, to revenge himself and to terrify ordinary people.
He is disowned by his father, who had given him the money, and he is prepared to hurt anyone who obstructs him.
The story suggests that science without moral responsibility destroys the scientist himself: Griffin ends up hunted, hungry and alone.
Wells thus warns that a discovery used for private gain instead of public good turns its maker into a criminal and a victim.

qa.q: Invisibility should have made Griffin powerful, but it made him helpless. Explain this paradox with two examples from the story.
a: First, at the inn in Iping, invisibility strands him: without clothes he is naked and freezing, with clothes he is visible and suspicious — the ‘headless’ reveal terrifies everyone and brings the police.
Second, he cannot eat, sleep or move unseen in a watched village; every theft leaves footprints, literally and figuratively.
The paradox is that invisibility removes his disguise but not his needs — science without planning is a trap, not a power.

qa.q: Was Griffin a brilliant scientist or a lawless person? Justify your answer.
a: **He was certainly a brilliant scientist.** He carried out experiment after experiment until he proved that the human body could be made invisible, and succeeded in swallowing drugs that made his body as transparent as glass. It is a discovery of extraordinary difficulty, and it shows real scientific ability and persistence.

**But he was also lawless.** His first use of the discovery was revenge: he set fire to his landlord's house because the man disliked him and was trying to eject him. He then robbed a shop in London, stole clothes from a big store, robbed a shopkeeper at Drury Lane, and attacked the village constable Mr Jaffers at Iping.

**Conclusion:** scientific brilliance without moral responsibility is dangerous. Griffin used a remarkable discovery for theft, revenge and violence, and ended up a hunted, homeless wanderer with no friends. So while his ability as a scientist cannot be denied, he was, in his behaviour, a lawless person.

qa.q: Is Griffin's invisibility a triumph of science or a source of danger in the story? Give a balanced answer using his discovery and his conduct.
a: Griffin's experiments show unusual scientific skill: he discovers how to make his body invisible, a remarkable achievement.
But the discovery does not make him wise or responsible. He burns his landlord's house and later steals clothes, food and money to survive.
At Iping, unexplained footprints and disturbances frighten people, while Griffin's temper and violence make the situation worse.
The story's balance is clear: scientific power can be impressive, but without self-control and concern for others it becomes a danger to society.

mcq.q: Griffin became invisible by: (a) an accident (b) swallowing certain rare drugs (c) a magic spell (d) a laboratory explosion
mcq.a: **(b) swallowing certain rare drugs** after many experiments.

mcq.q: The inn where Griffin stayed was at: (a) Drury Lane (b) London Bridge (c) Iping (d) Shotover
mcq.a: **(c) Iping**, where Mr and Mrs Hall kept the inn.

mcq.q: The village constable who tried to arrest Griffin was: (a) Mr Jaffers (b) Mr Hall (c) Mr Griffin (d) Mr Kemp
mcq.a: **(a) Mr Jaffers**, who was knocked unconscious by a man he could not see.

mcq.q: What does Griffin do to his landlord's house before leaving? (a) Sets it on fire (b) Turns it into an inn (c) Builds a laboratory in it (d) Sells its furniture
mcq.a: **(a) Sets it on fire.** Griffin's reckless actions put other people and their property in danger.

mcq.q: Why does Griffin take clothes after becoming invisible? (a) To disguise himself as a policeman (b) To sell them to a shopkeeper (c) To build a laboratory (d) To keep warm and move about in public
mcq.a: **(d) To keep warm and move about in public.** Invisibility leaves him exposed to the weather and unable to appear normally in public.

mcq.q: Griffin was a scientist who discovered: (a) how to fly  (b) a new gas  (c) how to make the human body transparent  (d) a cure for blindness
mcq.a: **(c) how to make the human body transparent.** He could not reverse the process, which ruined him.

mcq.q: Mrs Hall, the innkeeper, first grew suspicious when she saw: (a) footprints in the snow  (b) a broken window  (c) money missing from the till  (d) the stranger's bandaged head and his empty clothes moving
mcq.a: **(d) the stranger's bandaged head and his empty clothes.** The bandages hid the fact that he was invisible.

mcq.q: Griffin first betrayed his presence as: (a) a shadow on the wall (b) footprints appearing in the snow (c) a voice in the dark (d) smoke in the air
mcq.a: **(b) footprints appearing in the snow.** Two boys saw fresh footprints of bare feet where no man was visible.

title: The Making of a Scientist
short: Richard Ebright's projects, his curiosity and his mother's encouragement.
lede: A true account of how a scientist is made — curiosity, competition and a supportive parent.
lens: Short answers and a long answer on the qualities that make a scientist.
**Richard Ebright**, **the book *The Travels of Monarch X***, and **the twelve tiny gold spots on a monarch pupa** are the key details.
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Richard Ebright** grew up in Reading, Pennsylvania, an only child whose father died when he was in third grade. His mother was his only companion and encouraged his learning: she took him on trips, bought him scientific equipment and gave him challenges. She gave him a children's book, ***The Travels of Monarch X***, which opened the world of science to him; it was written by **James R. Wong**, and it described the migration of monarch butterflies to Central America. The book led him to raise butterflies in his basement, to tag them, and to write to the author, who sent him more suggestions. In the seventh grade he entered a county science fair with a project on monarch pupae, showing that the **twelve tiny gold spots on a monarch pupa** were not ornamental but were used to produce a hormone necessary for the butterfly's full development — he won, and was taken to the National Insect Collection. Later he discovered the **purpose of the gold spots**, worked on how cells work, and read the chemical structure of a hormone, which he and his college roommate **James R. Wong** described in a paper published in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*. He also became a champion debater and public speaker, a good canoeist and an expert photographer of nature and scientific exhibits. His teacher, **Richard A. Weiherer**, opened his mind to ideas and taught him to compete — not for the sake of winning, but to do the best job he could. Ebright says that his mother taught him that he must work hard to succeed, and that his interest in science came from her encouragement.

**2. Characters.** **Richard Ebright** — curious, persistent, competitive and well organised. **His mother** — the person who encouraged him, bought him equipment and gave him work to do. **Richard A. Weiherer** — his teacher, who opened his mind and taught him healthy competition. **James R. Wong** — the author of the book and later his co-researcher.
**3. Theme.** A scientist is made by **curiosity, a competitive spirit in the right sense, and the will to do the best work** — plus someone who encourages them.
tricks: - **Three qualities: curiosity, competitive spirit, first-rate mind.** Quote the textbook phrase if you can.
- The **twelve gold spots** produce a hormone — that discovery is the turning point of his career.
- His mother is the single most important influence; do not leave her out.
mistakes: - Saying his teacher encouraged him to compete in order to win. Weiherer taught him to compete **to do the best job he could**.
- Forgetting the mother. She is the answer to almost every 'who influenced him' question.
- Saying the gold spots were decorative. They **produce a hormone** necessary for full development.

qa.q: How did Richard Ebright's mother help him in his work?
qa.a: She was his only companion after his father's death, and she encouraged his learning in every way. She took him on trips, bought him telescopes, microscopes, cameras and other scientific equipment, and always found work for him to do. Most importantly she gave him the children's book The Travels of Monarch X, which opened the world of science to him and started him on his work with butterflies.

qa.q: What did Ebright discover about the twelve gold spots on a monarch pupa?
qa.a: He found that the twelve tiny gold spots on a monarch pupa were not merely ornamental, as was thought, but produced a hormone necessary for the full development of the butterfly. He demonstrated this by removing the spots and showing the effect, and the discovery won him the county science fair and a place at the National Insect Collection.

qa.q: What qualities go into the making of a scientist?
qa.a: According to the chapter, three things are needed: a first-rate mind, curiosity, and the will to win for the right reasons — not merely to win, but to do the best job one can. Richard Ebright had all three, and he also had the advantage of a mother who encouraged him and a teacher who opened his mind to ideas and taught him to compete in a healthy way.

qa.q: Richard Ebright's early science-fair entry did not win. Explain why that setback helped him become a better investigator.
a: At first he displayed collected butterfly specimens instead of asking a scientific question or testing an idea.
The result showed him that a science fair rewarded investigation, not simply a large collection.
He began designing experiments, learning from each project and asking questions that could be answered with evidence.

qa.q: A young student believes that winning is the only purpose of a science project. What lesson from Ebright's teacher and later work would you give the student?
a: Richard A. Weiherer taught Ebright to compete by doing the best job he could, not by winning at any cost.
Ebright's progress came from curiosity, careful experiments and learning from setbacks; the work mattered more than a prize.

qa.q: What did Richard Ebright learn from his monarch butterfly research?
a: He began by tagging monarch butterflies to track their migration to Mexico and beyond.
He discovered what caused a viral disease that kills nearly all monarchs, and later, with a friend, he found that the gold spots on the pupa are not decorative.
The spots produce a hormone needed for the full development of the butterfly.
This work won him the Searle scholarship, the Schering Plough award and a place in the Intel Science Talent Search.

qa.q: How did Ebright's failure at the county science fair in seventh grade help him later?
qa.a: Young Ebright exhibited slides of frog tissues — neat work, but only display, not experiment — and won nothing. The failure taught him what real science needs: a question, an experiment and an answer. Thereafter he did genuine investigations, starting with the viral disease of monarch caterpillars, and began winning every fair he entered.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

As a child, Ebright collected butterflies and entered a science fair with a display of specimens. He did not win. Later, he designed experiments and investigated questions about monarch butterflies, including the function of the gold spots on a pupa.

a: A display of specimens showed his collection but did not test a question or present an experiment.

title: The Necklace
short: Guy de Maupassant: an evening, a lost necklace and ten years of debt.
lede: The most famous ironic ending in the syllabus. Learn the figures — 40,000 francs and ten years.
lens: Short answers and a value-based question on whether Matilda's suffering was deserved.
**Matilda Loisel**, the **Ministry ball**, and the necklace worth **36,000 francs** replaced at **40,000**.
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Matilda Loisel** was a pretty and charming girl born into a family of clerks, married to a clerk at the Board of Education. She was unhappy, believing she was born for all the delicacies and luxuries of life, and she suffered from the poverty of her home. Her husband brought home an invitation to a reception at the **Ministry of Public Instruction**. Instead of being delighted she was irritated, because she had no suitable dress and no jewels. Her husband gave her **four hundred francs** he had saved for a gun, and she borrowed a **superb diamond necklace** from her rich friend **Madame Forestier**. At the ball she was the prettiest of all, elegant, smiling and quite above herself with happiness. On the way home she found the necklace was **lost**. The Loisels searched everywhere, then bought a new one for **forty thousand francs**, eighteen thousand of which her husband had inherited and the rest borrowed at ruinous interest. They spent **ten years** repaying the debt: they dismissed their maid, changed their lodgings, and Matilda did the heavy housework while her husband worked evenings and did copying at twopence-halfpenny a page. After ten years everything was paid. Matilda, now old and hard-looking, met Madame Forestier in the Champs-Élysées and told her the whole story. Madame Forestier, moved, took her hands and said: *'Oh, my poor Matilda! But mine was only paste! It was worth at most five hundred francs!'*

**2. Characters.** **Matilda** — pretty, discontented, vain, and ultimately hardworking and honest in paying the debt. **M. Loisel** — kind, contented, self-sacrificing; he gives up his gun money and works for ten years to pay her debt. **Madame Forestier** — rich, generous, and the unknowing cause of the disaster.
**3. Theme.** Discontent and vanity can cost a whole life; and appearances are deceptive — what looked like a diamond necklace was only paste.
tricks: - **Two figures: 36,000 francs for the necklace and 40,000 to replace it; ten years to repay.**
- The final line — *'mine was only paste'* — is the irony. Always quote it.
- Matilda is not simply a villain: she pays the debt honestly for ten years. Say both halves.
mistakes: - Saying Matilda stole the necklace. It was **lost**, not stolen.
- Giving the replacement cost as 36,000 francs. The new necklace cost **40,000**.
- Forgetting M. Loisel's sacrifice — he gave up his gun and worked for ten years.

qa.q: Why was Matilda unhappy with her life?
qa.a: Because she believed she was born for all the delicacies and luxuries of life, and her actual life was poor and plain. She suffered from the poverty of her home, from the shabby walls, the worn chairs and the ugly curtains, and she dreamed of silent antechambers, tall bronze candelabra and expensive dinners. Her dissatisfaction came from comparing herself with the rich, so she could not enjoy what she had.

qa.q: What was the effect of losing the necklace on the Loisels' lives?
qa.a: They had to replace it, and a similar necklace cost forty thousand francs. Her husband used the eighteen thousand francs his father had left him and borrowed the rest at ruinous interest. For ten years they lived in poverty: they dismissed their maid, moved to a garret, and Matilda did all the heavy housework while her husband worked evenings and did copying at twopence-halfpenny a page. Matilda grew old, rough and hard-looking, and they lost their youth and their comfort to pay a debt they need never have had.

qa.q: Matilda borrows jewellery to appear wealthy for one evening. Explain how her desire to impress others helps bring about the long hardship that follows.
a: Matilda feels dissatisfied with her ordinary life and believes that luxury and admiration are what she deserves.
She borrows Madame Forestier's necklace to complete the appearance she wants at the reception, then loses it.
The replacement costs far more than she can afford, and the Loisels spend ten years repaying the debt; the wish to seem rich transforms their lives.

qa.q: The Loisels work for years to replace the necklace without telling Madame Forestier the truth. What more honest choice could they have made, and what might it have changed?
a: They could have told Madame Forestier promptly that the necklace was lost and asked her what it was worth or how to replace it.
That conversation might have revealed that the original was imitation jewellery, avoiding the enormous loan and years of hardship.

qa.q: What was the price of the lost necklace and how did the Loisels pay for it?
a: They borrowed 18,000 francs from usurers to buy a replacement necklace that cost 36,000 francs.
For ten years they dismissed their maid, moved to a garret, and Matilda did all the housework while her husband worked evenings and night.
He copied manuscripts at five sous a page and often worked late into the night; at the end of ten years they had paid back everything.
The price was not only money: Matilda lost her youth, her beauty and her comfortable life, and became a hard, coarse woman.

qa.q: Why did Matilda borrow a necklace instead of wearing flowers, as her husband suggested? What does this choice reveal?
qa.a: Her husband suggested natural flowers, which would have been pretty and honest — but Matilda wanted to look rich, not pretty. She borrowed the diamond necklace from Mme Forestier because her dream was to be envied by the other women at the ball. The choice reveals her pride: she would rather borrow glamour than admit her real position.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Matilda attends the reception wearing a borrowed necklace and enjoys being admired. On returning home, she discovers that it is missing. The Loisels buy a replacement and spend ten years paying off the debt, only to learn that the original necklace was paste.

(a) Why did Matilda borrow the necklace?
(b) What decision creates the years of hardship?
(c) What makes the ending ironic?
a: She wants to look prosperous and elegant at the reception and believes the jewels will complete her appearance.
The Loisels replace the necklace without first checking its value with Madame Forestier, and the replacement costs 40,000 francs.
They sacrifice ten years to repay the price of a real-looking replacement, then learn that the original was imitation jewellery worth very little.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

After losing the borrowed necklace, the Loisels choose not to explain what happened to Madame Forestier. They buy a costly replacement and accept years of work and debt. When Matilda later meets her friend, the truth changes how she understands the sacrifice.

(a) What does the Loisels' silence cause?
(b) What does Matilda learn from Madame Forestier?
(c) What is the story's warning about appearances?
a: Their silence prevents them from discovering the original necklace's true value and leads them to take on an unnecessary debt.
Madame Forestier reveals that the original necklace was paste, not genuine diamonds.
A valuable appearance may be deceptive; the Loisels' belief about the jewels changes their lives more than the actual object did.

qa.q: Explain the twist at the end of ‘The Necklace' and what it says about pride.
a: When they meet again, Mme Forestier does not at first recognise Matilda, who looks old and worn.
Matilda tells her the truth, and Mme Forestier reveals that the original necklace was paste, worth only 500 francs.
So ten years of sacrifice were spent replacing an imitation, while the borrowed glitter of one evening cost them everything.
Maupassant's point is that vanity and the desire to appear rich punished them far more than poverty itself did.

qa.q: Matilda's husband works evenings, borrows at ruinous rates and never complains. What does the story gain by making him, not Matilda, the silent sufferer?
a: His silent suffering measures the true cost of Matilda's vanity — the debt falls on the one person who never wanted luxury.
It also keeps the reader's sympathy balanced: Matilda causes the disaster, but her husband's loyalty makes the ten years of poverty moving rather than merely deserved.
Without him the story would be a fable about pride; with him it becomes a tragedy about love paying for pride.

qa.q: Was Matilda's suffering deserved? Give reasons for your answer.
a: **The case that it was deserved:** her suffering came from her own vanity and discontent. She had a kind husband who loved her and a comfortable enough life, but she could not enjoy either because she compared herself with the rich. She was embarrassed to borrow a dress, insisted on jewels for the ball, and was so anxious to escape quickly that she did not check the necklace. Her vanity caused the loss.

**The case that it was not deserved:** she never stole anything, and she behaved honourably afterwards. Rather than admit the loss to her friend, she and her husband replaced the necklace honestly and spent ten years repaying a ruinous debt. She did the heavy housework and gave up her looks and her youth. A mistake of vanity, however foolish, does not deserve ten years of punishment.

**Conclusion:** the punishment was far greater than the fault, and that disproportion is what makes the ending so bitter. The real tragedy is that the necklace was only paste, so the ten years of suffering were wasted entirely.

qa.q: How does Maupassant use Matilda's desire for status and the final revelation to make “The Necklace” a story about the cost of appearances?
a: Matilda is unhappy because she imagines herself suited to luxury and feels ashamed of her modest home and clothes.
At the reception, the borrowed necklace helps her appear wealthy, but after it goes missing the Loisels hide the truth and buy an expensive replacement.
They spend ten years working and sacrificing to repay 40,000 francs, believing they are replacing valuable diamonds.
Madame Forestier's final revelation that the original was paste makes the sacrifice tragic and ironic: appearances deceive Matilda, but also the couple's fear and silence deepen the cost.

mcq.q: 'The Necklace' is written by: (a) Anton Chekhov (b) Ruskin Bond (c) H. G. Wells (d) Guy de Maupassant
mcq.a: **(d) Guy de Maupassant**, the French short-story writer.

mcq.q: The necklace the Loisels bought to replace the lost one cost: (a) 18,000 francs (b) 36,000 francs (c) 40,000 francs (d) 500 francs
mcq.a: **(c) forty thousand francs** — eighteen thousand inherited and the rest borrowed.

mcq.q: The original necklace belonging to Madame Forestier was: (a) a real diamond necklace worth 36,000 francs (b) stolen (c) never found (d) paste, worth at most 500 francs
mcq.a: **(d) paste, worth at most five hundred francs** — the irony revealed in the last line.

mcq.q: Why does Matilda borrow jewellery from Madame Forestier? (a) She wants to appear elegant at the reception (b) She plans to sell it at a market (c) Her husband asks her to repair it (d) She wants to give it to her sister
mcq.a: **(a) She wants to appear elegant at the reception.** Matilda believes the jewellery will complete the prosperous appearance she wants.

mcq.q: Which ministry sends the invitation to the reception? (a) The Ministry of War (b) The Ministry of Public Instruction (c) The Ministry of Trade (d) The Ministry of Agriculture
mcq.a: **(b) The Ministry of Public Instruction.** M. Loisel brings home an invitation from the ministry where he works.

mcq.q: Matilda borrowed the necklace from: (a) Mme Forestier  (b) her sister  (c) her mother  (d) a shop
mcq.a: **(a) Mme Forestier.** Her rich friend lent her what Matilda believed were real diamonds.

mcq.q: The Loisels spent how many years repaying the debt? (a) five  (b) twenty  (c) ten  (d) two
mcq.a: **(c) ten.** At the end of ten years Mme Loisel looked old and worn out.

mcq.q: The dress Matilda's husband gave her money for cost: (a) 4,000 francs (b) 400 francs (c) 40 francs (d) 40,000 francs
mcq.a: **(b) 400 francs.** He had been saving it for a gun — and gave it up for her ball dress.
