title: Bholi
short: K. A. Abbas: a neglected girl finds her voice through education.
lede: The transformation from Bholi to Sulekha. The rejection of the dowry is the turning point.
lens: Short answers and a value-based question on how education changed her, and on the dowry.
**Bholi / Sulekha**, the **pock marks**, **Bishamber Nath**, and the **teacher** are the key names.
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Bholi**, whose real name was **Sulekha**, was the fourth daughter of **Ramlal**, the village *numberdar*. She fell off the cot as a child and was disfigured on one side of her face, and later an attack of **smallpox** left black pock marks all over her body. She was neglected, given coarse clothes, and never sent to school. She was slow to speak and stammered, so the other children mocked her, and she became silent. Then the **tehsildar** asked Ramlal, as a revenue official, to set an example by sending his daughters to school, so Bholi was sent to the village school. There her **teacher** was kind and encouraging: she told Bholi that if she came to school every day she would learn more than anyone in the village, and would speak without stammering. Bholi began to read, and her confidence grew. When she was of marriageable age, **Bishamber Nath**, a prosperous grocer from another village — lame, with a grown-up family — came to see her. He agreed to the match, but at the wedding ceremony the veil slipped from Bholi's face and he saw her pock-marked face; he demanded **five thousand rupees** as compensation. Ramlal, humiliated, begged, but Bishamber Nath refused to lower the demand. At that moment **Bholi**, who had been silent throughout, spoke clearly and without a stammer: she threw the **garland of yellow marigolds** into the fire and refused to marry such a mean, greedy and contemptible coward. She then said she would serve her parents in their old age and teach in the same school where she had learnt so much.

**2. Characters.** **Bholi (Sulekha)** — neglected and mocked, transformed by kindness and education into a confident young woman. **The teacher** — the turning figure; her encouragement gives Bholi a voice. **Ramlal and his wife** — parents who neglected her, though her father is not cruel. **Bishamber Nath** — a lame, prosperous, greedy grocer who demands dowry.
**3. Themes.** The **transforming power of education and kindness**; the **evils of dowry**; and the **rights of girls**, especially those who are differently abled or considered unattractive.
tricks: - **Two names: Bholi and Sulekha.** The shift from one to the other is the story.
- She rejects the marriage **by speaking clearly** — no stammer. That detail is the proof of her transformation.
- The **garland of yellow marigolds thrown into the fire** is the most quoted image.
mistakes: - Saying Bholi's parents hated her. They **neglected** her; her father was not cruel.
- Saying Bishamber Nath was handsome and young. He is **lame and has grown-up children**.
- Missing the ending: she decides to **teach in the same school**.

qa.q: How did the teacher transform Bholi's life?
qa.a: The teacher was the first person to treat Bholi with kindness and respect. She spoke to her in a soft, soothing voice, told her not to be afraid, and promised that if she came to school every day she would learn more than anyone else in the village and would soon speak without a stammer. She encouraged Bholi to read, praised her progress, and gave her confidence. Education gave Bholi a voice, self-respect and the courage to refuse a humiliating marriage.

qa.q: Why did Bholi refuse to marry Bishamber Nath?
qa.a: Because at the wedding, when her veil slipped and he saw her pock-marked face, he demanded five thousand rupees as compensation and refused to marry her without it. He had already agreed to the match when he thought she was fair, so his demand showed that he was mean, greedy and contemptible. Bholi, who had been silent until then, spoke clearly and without a stammer and refused to marry such a coward.

qa.q: What does the story say about the value of girls' education?
qa.a: It shows that education can transform a neglected, mocked and silent girl into a confident person with self-respect. Before school, Bholi was slow to speak, was laughed at and had no self-worth. After school, she could read, spoke without a stammer, and was able to stand up against a greedy bridegroom and his dowry demand. She finally decides to serve her parents and teach in the school where she learnt so much — so education gives her both independence and a purpose.

qa.q: Bholi is mocked for stammering and marked by smallpox, but she ultimately refuses a humiliating marriage. Explain how education helps her make that choice.
a: Her teacher treats her kindly and encourages her to speak, so school gives Bholi confidence as well as lessons.
By the wedding, she can recognise Bishamber's demand for dowry as an insult and injustice, not a fate she must accept.
She refuses the marriage and chooses to support herself by teaching, showing how education gives her a voice and independence.

qa.q: Ramlal sends Bholi to school because the tehsildar asks the village officials to set an example. Explain how this unexpected start changes Bholi's future.
a: Bholi begins school reluctantly, but her teacher's patience helps her overcome silence and stammering.
Education gives her confidence to reject Bishamber when he demands dowry, and she chooses a life of dignity rather than an unjust marriage.

qa.q: Why is Bholi called a simpleton, and how does she change?
a: As a child she fell and damaged part of her brain, so she was slow, stammered and was mocked as ‘Bholi, the simpleton'.
She was neglected, given old clothes and little food, and kept out of school for years.
The village primary school and then the city school gave her a teacher's kindness, confidence and the ability to speak without stammering.
By the end she is able to refuse an unequal marriage and to speak up for her father, her teacher and herself.

qa.q: Why was Bholi sent to school when her parents did not value girls' education?
qa.a: The tehsildar had ordered Ramlal, the numberdar, to set an example by sending his daughters to school, and Ramlal dared not disobey. Since Bholi — pock-marked, stammering, considered a simpleton — was the least valued child and unlikely to marry, her parents sacrificed her to the school while keeping her sisters at home. Neglect, ironically, gave her the chance that changed her life.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

At school, Bholi is frightened and stammers. Her teacher does not mock her; she speaks gently and encourages Bholi to try again. Years later, at her wedding, Bishamber demands money after seeing her face, and Bholi refuses to marry him.

(a) What does the teacher's response give Bholi?
(b) What prompts Bholi's refusal at the wedding?
(c) How has Bholi changed?
a: The teacher gives her patience, encouragement and a safe place to speak without being ridiculed.
Bishamber demands dowry after seeing her pock-marked face; Bholi rejects his greed and the disrespect shown to her family.
She grows from a frightened, silent girl into a confident young woman able to speak for herself and choose her future.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Bholi's parents once think that she is unlikely to marry and do not expect much from her. At the end, she refuses Bishamber's dowry demand and tells her father that she will teach at the school.

(a) What does Bholi's final decision reject?
(b) What future does she choose?
(c) Why is this ending important to the story's message?
a: She rejects the idea that she must accept a disrespectful marriage because of her appearance or the family's fear of social shame.
She chooses to earn a living and become a teacher at the school that helped her.
Her education has given her a voice and agency; the ending challenges dowry and the neglect of girls while affirming her right to decide.

qa.q: How does education give Bholi a voice?
a: Her teacher's encouragement makes her believe she can learn; she is given books, a clean dress and, above all, attention.
Education gives her self-respect: she learns to read, write and do sums, and she stops stammering in front of others.
When Bishamber Nath demands five thousand rupees as dowry, she understands that she is being bought and tears up the wedding garland.
She finally declares that she will serve her parents and teach at the same school, showing that education has turned a frightened child into a person with a will of her own.

qa.q: Bholi throws the wedding garland into the fire. Why is this gesture the climax of the story?
a: The garland stands for the marriage her parents arranged at any price — even a 5,000-rupee dowry to a middle-aged widower.
By throwing it into the fire, Bholi burns not just one wedding but the whole bargain: dowry, obedience and the idea that a girl is a burden.
It is the climax because the stammering simpleton now speaks clearly and chooses for herself — education has given her a voice, and she uses it.

qa.q: How does Bholi's journey from a fearful child to an independent young woman challenge the way her family and society judge her?
a: Her family treats Bholi as a burden because she is shy, stammers and has smallpox marks, while others mock her as a simpleton.
At school, her teacher offers kindness and patient encouragement. Bholi gradually gains confidence and learns to speak without fear.
At the wedding, Bishamber demands dowry after noticing her face. Bholi refuses to let the demand or her family's anxiety decide her worth.

By choosing to teach, she becomes independent and uses her voice. The story argues that education can transform opportunity and that a girl's dignity is not measured by appearance or marriage prospects.

mcq.q: Bholi's real name was: (a) Sunita (b) Kamla (c) Sulekha (d) Rukmini
mcq.a: **(c) Sulekha** — Bholi was the name she was given because she was considered simple.

mcq.q: Bholi's face was pock-marked because of: (a) an attack of smallpox (b) a fall from the cot (c) a burn (d) a skin disease
mcq.a: **(a) an attack of smallpox**, which left black pock marks all over her body.

mcq.q: Bishamber Nath demanded five thousand rupees because: (a) he was poor (b) he saw Bholi's pock-marked face (c) her father refused (d) the priest demanded it
mcq.a: **(b) he saw Bholi's pock-marked face** when her veil slipped at the wedding.

mcq.q: What quality in Bholi's teacher helps her begin to speak with confidence? (a) Threats and punishment (b) Patience and encouragement (c) Silence about her progress (d) A promise of marriage
mcq.a: **(b) Patience and encouragement.** The teacher's kindness helps Bholi feel safe enough to learn.

mcq.q: What does Bholi choose to do after refusing Bishamber? (a) Leave the village alone (b) Return to the wedding ceremony (c) Stop learning (d) Teach at the school
mcq.a: **(d) Teach at the school.** She chooses useful work and independence rather than the dowry marriage.

mcq.q: Bholi's real name is: (a) Sulekha  (b) Bholi  (c) Mangla  (d) Radha
mcq.a: **(a) Sulekha.** She was called Bholi, meaning the simpleton, because of her looks and her slowness.

mcq.q: Bholi refuses to marry Bishamber Nath because he: (a) is poor  (b) is uneducated  (c) demands dowry from her father after the garlands are exchanged  (d) is a widower
mcq.a: **(c) demands dowry from her father after the garlands are exchanged.** She throws the garland into the fire.

mcq.q: Bishamber Nath, the bridegroom Ramlal finds for Bholi, was: (a) a young schoolteacher (b) a rich landlord (c) a doctor (d) a middle-aged grocer and widower from another village
mcq.a: **(d) a middle-aged grocer and widower from another village.** He limped, had grown-up children — and demanded five thousand rupees on seeing Bholi's face.

title: The Book That Saved the Earth
short: Claire Boiko: Martians misread a nursery rhyme and abandon an invasion.
lede: A comic science-fiction play. Learn the three Martians and the nursery book.
lens: Short answers; know **Think-Tank**, **Captain Omega**, **Noodle**, **Sergeant Oop**, and ***Mother Goose***.
The **twenty-fifth century** is called the *Era of the Book*.
concepts: **1. Summary.** The play is set in the twenty-fifth century, described as the **Era of the Book**, when books were used for everything. The Historian tells how, in the year 2040, the people of Mars had planned to invade Earth, but the invasion was called off because of a book. The Martian **Think-Tank**, the Commander-in-Chief of the Space Probe fleet, is vain and stupid, and believes he is the most intelligent creature in the universe. He sends **Captain Omega**, **Lieutenant Iota** and **Sergeant Oop** to Earth to make contact. They land in a library and find books. Think-Tank, examining the book from the control room, mistakes it for an **earth sandwich** and orders them to eat it; when they cannot, he decides that the books are **communication devices** and that the earthlings use them to communicate by ear. He orders Noodle to give the crew **vitamins** so that they can hear the books. The crew then reads ***Mother Goose*** aloud. When Sergeant Oop reads *'Mistress Mary, quite contrary, how does your garden grow?'* with silver bells and cockle shells, Think-Tank concludes that the earthlings grow **metals and explosives** in their gardens. When he hears *'Hey diddle diddle, the cat and the fiddle, the cow jumped over the moon'* and the picture of a cow, he panics, believing that the earthlings have taught their animals a high culture of music and space techniques, and that they are planning to attack **Mars Central Control**. Terrified, he orders the crew to leave Earth at once, and later flees to **Alpha Centauri**, a hundred million miles away. The Historian ends by saying that this is how the book saved the Earth — the Martians abandoned the invasion because of their misunderstanding of a nursery rhyme, and afterwards the Martians and the earthlings became friends, and Mars is now called *New Earth*.

**2. Characters.** **Think-Tank** — the vain, stupid, boastful Commander-in-Chief of Mars. **Noodle** — his clever, modest apprentice, who politely corrects him. **Captain Omega, Lieutenant Iota, Sergeant Oop** — the crew of the space probe. **The Historian and Miss Twist** — the narrators of the twenty-fifth century.
**3. Theme.** Ignorance and arrogance lead to comic misjudgement; books are powerful; and understanding, not force, brings peace.
tricks: - **Think-Tank is stupid and Noodle is clever** — but Noodle lets Think-Tank take the credit. That contrast is the joke.
- Three misreadings in order: book = sandwich, book = ear communication device, nursery rhyme = military threat.
- The Era of the Book is the **twenty-fifth century**; the invasion was planned for **2040**.
mistakes: - Saying the Martians attacked. They **fled**, to Alpha Centauri, a hundred million miles away.
- Calling Noodle stupid. He is the **clever** one; Think-Tank is the fool.
- Forgetting the ending: Mars and Earth become friends, and Mars is renamed **New Earth**.

qa.q: Why did Think-Tank mistake the book for an earth sandwich?
qa.a: Because the Martians had never seen a book. Think-Tank examined it from the control room, saw that it was flat and had pages, and concluded that the earthlings ate it as a sandwich. He ordered the crew to eat it, and when they could not, he changed his mind and decided that the books were communication devices used for listening.

qa.q: How did the book save the Earth?
qa.a: Because the Martians misunderstood what they read. When Sergeant Oop read 'Mistress Mary, quite contrary', with its silver bells and cockle shells, Think-Tank concluded that the earthlings grew metals and explosives in their gardens. When he heard about the cow jumping over the moon, he believed that the earthlings had taught their animals a high culture of music and space techniques, and that they planned to attack Mars Central Control. Terrified, he ordered the crew to leave Earth at once and later fled to Alpha Centauri — so the invasion was called off, and the Earth was saved by a nursery rhyme.

qa.q: Describe Think-Tank's character.
qa.a: He is the Commander-in-Chief of the Space Probe fleet of Mars, and he believes himself to be the most powerful and intelligent creature in the universe. In fact he is vain, boastful and stupid: he mistakes a book for a sandwich, cannot understand a nursery rhyme, and panics at the idea of a cow jumping over the moon. He is also a coward, since he flees to Alpha Centauri, a hundred million miles away, at the first sign of danger.

qa.q: Think-Tank believes the nursery book reveals a dangerous Earth army. Explain how his arrogance turns simple rhymes into a false military report.
a: Think-Tank assumes that his first interpretation must be correct and dismisses the possibility that the book is for children.
He reads nursery images such as “mistress Mary” and “silver bells” as references to weapons, technology or military threats.
His crew's fear grows from his confident but mistaken readings, so the planned invasion is abandoned.

qa.q: Noodle offers suggestions to Think-Tank without openly challenging him. Explain how this careful manner helps Noodle and the crew.
a: Noodle phrases corrections as respectful possibilities, allowing Think-Tank to accept the advice without admitting he has been wrong.
His quiet intelligence helps the crew interpret the book more sensibly and later helps avert the Martian invasion.

qa.q: How do the Martians misunderstand the nursery rhymes?
a: Think-Tank asks to be shown books, and the crew bring him nursery rhymes from a library.
From ‘Mistress Mary, quite contrary' he decides that humans grow money, and from ‘Mother Goose' he concludes that she is the supreme ruler of Earth.
He takes the rhyme about the cow that jumped over the moon as proof that Earth's creatures can jump between planets.
Finally he hears ‘Humpty Dumpty' and ‘Hey diddle diddle' and decides that Earth is planning to launch an attack on Mars.

qa.q: How does Noodle's character contrast with Think-Tank's? Why is this contrast important to the play?
a: Think-Tank is vain, boastful and stupid — he mistakes a book for a sandwich and nursery rhymes for threats. Noodle, his apprentice, is clever and modest — he quietly suggests the right ideas (that the book is for reading) and lets his master take the credit.
The contrast drives both the humour and the ending: folly commands, wisdom obeys, until folly flees to Alpha Centauri and Noodle's line — Mars and Earth as friends — wins.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

The Martian probe studies a book of nursery rhymes. Think-Tank treats ordinary images as evidence of Earth's power; “silver bells” and other harmless words become military equipment in his interpretation. Noodle makes careful suggestions, but Think-Tank remains certain of his own brilliance.

(a) What has Think-Tank misunderstood?
(b) How does his confidence affect the crew?
(c) What does Noodle's manner reveal about him?
a: He mistakes a children's book and its playful rhymes for a literal account of Earth's weapons and military strength.
The crew accepts his claims and becomes frightened, even though the evidence is being misread.
Noodle is intelligent and tactful: he offers a better interpretation indirectly so that the arrogant commander can accept it.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

The invasion force abandons its plan after Think-Tank interprets Mother Goose rhymes as dangerous instructions. The crew has not tested his readings against the book's purpose; Noodle's modest comments are the only gentle challenge.

(a) Why do the Martians retreat?
(b) What reasoning error causes their fear?
(c) How does the play use this mistake for comedy?
a: They believe Earth has powerful weapons and that an invasion would be unsafe, so they retreat to Mars.
They take figurative, childlike rhymes literally and accept Think-Tank's guesses without checking them.
The audience recognises the harmless nursery references while the Martians imagine a terrifying arsenal; the gap between the two readings creates dramatic irony.

qa.q: What is the humour in the way the Martians abandon their invasion?
a: Their invasion is decided by a commander who is certain he is the greatest intellect in the universe but cannot read a simple rhyme.
The more evidence he gets, the more absurd his conclusions become: library shelves become ‘sandwiches' and books are ‘communication sandwiches'.
He panics, orders the fleet to retreat and abandons the invasion of a planet whose only weapons were a cow, a dish and a spoon.
The joke is that the greatest danger to Earth was never an attack from Mars, but a Martian commander too proud to ask what the words mean.

qa.q: ‘Silver bells and cockle shells’ become metals and explosives in Martian eyes. Explain two such misreadings and the panic each causes.
a: First, ‘mistress Mary, quite contrary’ with her silver bells and cockle shells is read as an earthling growing metals and explosives — proof that earthlings farm weapons.
Second, ‘Humpty Dumpty had a great fall’ is read as Earth's plan for Think-Tank himself: ‘he will have a great fall’ sends the commander into panic.
Each rhyme the Martians decode raises the alarm, until Think-Tank orders the invasion abandoned — a book of rhymes defeats an army.

qa.q: How does the play make a nursery-rhyme book powerful enough to stop an invasion, and what does it suggest about leadership?
a: Think-Tank's crew finds a book of nursery rhymes, but the arrogant commander does not understand its purpose or language.
He interprets ordinary images as evidence of advanced weapons. The crew trusts his confidence, so a string of mistaken readings becomes a threat in their minds.
Noodle is the more perceptive leader: he suggests corrections politely, while Think-Tank's vanity prevents him from checking his assumptions.
The Martians retreat from a danger that exists only in their interpretation. The comedy warns that authority without humility or evidence can turn a harmless text into a crisis.

mcq.q: 'The Book That Saved the Earth' is written by: (a) Guy de Maupassant (b) Claire Boiko (c) Victor Canning (d) H. G. Wells
mcq.a: **(b) Claire Boiko**, and it is written as a play.

mcq.q: Think-Tank first mistakes the book for: (a) an earth sandwich (b) a mirror (c) a weapon (d) a map
mcq.a: **(a) an earth sandwich**, and he orders the crew to eat it.

mcq.q: The book that frightened Think-Tank was: (a) the Bible (b) Mother Goose (c) an atlas (d) a Martian history
mcq.a: **(b) Mother Goose**, a book of nursery rhymes.

mcq.q: Who is Think-Tank's apprentice and the more perceptive adviser? (a) Noodle (b) Captain Omega (c) Lieutenant Iota (d) Sergeant Oop
mcq.a: **(a) Noodle.** He offers careful suggestions that help reveal the crew's misinterpretations.

mcq.q: What name is given to Mars after the events of the play? (a) The Era of War (b) Little Earth (c) New Earth (d) The Book World
mcq.a: **(c) New Earth.** The story ends with Mars and Earth becoming friends, and Mars taking the name New Earth.

mcq.q: The commander of the Martian invasion force was: (a) Noodle  (b) Omega  (c) Think-Tank  (d) Iota
mcq.a: **(c) Think-Tank.** His assistant Noodle is the one who actually understands the books.

mcq.q: The Martians decided that Earth was dangerous after reading: (a) a newspaper  (b) a scientific journal  (c) a history book  (d) nursery rhymes
mcq.a: **(d) nursery rhymes.** ‘Humpty Dumpty' and ‘Hey diddle diddle' convinced them that Earth was attacking Mars.

mcq.q: The play is set in: (a) the twentieth century (b) the twenty-first century (c) ancient times (d) the twenty-fifth century, the Era of the Book
mcq.a: **(d) the twenty-fifth century, the Era of the Book.** A historian of that age stages the story as a history play.

steps: 1. Set the **frame**: it is a play-within-a-play, with the Historian addressing the audience from the twenty-fifth century.
2. Describe the **Martian invasion** — Think-Tank, Noodle, Captain Omega, and the book *Mother Goose* that is mistaken for a battle plan.

4. Close with the **joke** — the Martians flee from a nursery rhyme, and the book is marked with a red triangle as a dangerous weapon.
